title: Integrated Workflow for Phosphopeptide Identification in NK Cells and Targets During Immunological Synapse Formation
author: Perez-Hernandez, Filali, et al.
materials: Precision Plus Protein™ Dual Color Standards

Proteins are separated on a pre-casted SDS gel into three fractions to decrease the complexity of the sample. A lower complexity will increase the number of identified phosphopeptides. The SDS-gel functions two-fold: first, the heating of the samples reverses the PFA cross-links, and second, it removes substances that are interfering with the mass spectrometric analysis. Proteins are digested into peptides in the SDS-gel, and the resulting peptides are extracted. The contained phospho-peptides are enriched using metallo-chelate chromatography before being analyzed by mass spectrometry.Note: The starting material should not be below 0.35∗106 cell-to-cell conjugates, which approximately corresponds to 25 μg per sample.31.SDS-Page setup.a.Place the Bis-Tris gel in the tank.b.Fill the tank with running buffer.32.Sample cleaning and fractionation by SDS-PAGE.a.Resuspend the PFA-treated samples in 25 μL 2× Laemmli buffer and add 5 μL 10% SDS.b.Vortex vigorous for 20 s.c.Incubate 10 min at 95°C.d.Put the samples on ice for 5 min.e.Centrifuge for 10 min at maximum speed in a tabletop centrifuge (16,000 × g).f.Load the samples and protein size standard in the different wells.g.Program the power supply to 120 V constant per gel.h.Run the gel until the running front reaches approximately half of the gel.i.Stain the gel with Coomassie brilliant blue staining solution.j.Cut each lane with a razor blade in three equal slices. Every slice should be cut into cubes of approximately 1 mm2 size to optimize further cleaning and increase penetration of the different reagents.k.Place all cubes from every slice in a different 2 mL Eppendorf tube.Note: Proteins should be clearly fractionated into different bands. See problem 4.Note: The whole sample should run through the gel with no remaining sample at the top of the well. See problem 5.33.Protein digestion.a.Wash the gel pieces with 400 μL of washing buffer A for 10 min in a thermomixer, 800 g, at RT.b.Discard the supernatant.c.Wash the gel pieces with 400 μL of washing buffer B for 10 min in a thermomixer, 800 × g, at RT.d.Discard the supernatant.e.Repeat the steps (33a to 33c) four times.f.After discarding the supernatant, incubate the sample with 200 μL of reduction buffer for 20 min in a thermomixer at 800 × g.g.Discard the supernatant.h.Add 200 μL of alkylation buffer for 30 min in a thermomixer at 800 × g (in the dark) at RT.i.Discard the supernatant.j.Add 200 μL washing buffer B for 10 min in a thermomixer at 800 × g.k.Discard the supernatant.l.Add 150 μL digestion buffer.m.Incubate the samples for 16 h at 37°C.n.Stop the digestion by adding 15 μL of stop buffer (final concentration 0.1% formic acid).o.Place the supernatant in a fresh 2 mL Eppendorf tube.p.Add 150 μL of ST buffer C to the gel pieces and incubate the sample for 30 min at 800 g at RT.q.Pool the supernatant from the gel pieces with the previous extraction in the Eppendorf tubes.r.Dry the samples in a speed-vac for 2 h at 45°C.

The recorded mass spectrometric data has to be matched to peptides and proteins. For this, we use the MaxQuant software package. MaxQuant demands significant computing resources. In our case, we used a 72-core computer to analyze the data. Using a smaller computer will prolong the time needed for the analysis.37.Inject 0.2–0.5 μg of material into an LC-MS/MS. It is very important to inject exactly the same amount in all the samples (peptide abundance measured by Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit).Note: the parameters that are described below are a guide for a specific mass spectrometer, but others could be used to perform MS analysis.Optional: The amount of phosphopeptides to inject could differ depending on the peptide abundance, the mass spectrometer, and the nanoHPLC system. Those conditions have to be adjusted injecting the corresponding volume into LC-MS/MS. For a Q Exactive HF (Thermo Scientific) 0.1 μg of material is enough to generate a robust dataset (around 2,500 peptides per measurement, which corresponds to approximately 2 × 109 of maximum total ion count (TIC)).

The MaxQuant search engine generates several files while processing the raw data from ThermoFisher instruments. To extract the files needed for the analysis: go to the combined folder, and then to the txt folder. The samples are analyzed by R-based programming or Perseus.18,19 Perseus is convenient for filtering data (114–116). For the quantification (117–121) we recommend R-based scripting to analyze the data. An example of the data analysis is shown in Table S1.38.Filter out the phosphopeptides belonging to proteins that are contaminants, reverse or identified by site in proteinGroups.txt file and Phospho (STY)Sites.txt file.39.In Phospho (STY)Sites.txt file, Phosphopeptides with at least two individual SILAC ratios in each type of sample can be selected with the following threshold parameters:a.score > 40.b.score for localization > 40.c.PEP 5

steps.title: Set up SDS-PAGE gel
steps.instruction: Place the Bis‑Tris gel into the electrophoresis tank and fill the tank with running buffer.

substeps.instruction: a. Place the Bis‑Tris gel in the tank.
b. Fill the tank with running buffer.

steps.title: Prepare and load samples for SDS-PAGE
steps.instruction: Resuspend PFA‑treated samples, denature, load onto the gel, run, stain, and cut the gel into three equal slices and 1 mm³ cubes, keeping each slice in a separate tube.

substeps.instruction: a. Resuspend each sample in 25 µL 2× Laemmli buffer and add 5 µL 10 % SDS.
b. Vortex vigorously for 20 s.
c. Incubate 10 min at 95 °C.
d. Place on ice for 5 min.
e. Centrifuge 10 min at maximum speed (≈16 000 × g) in a tabletop centrifuge.
f. Load the cleared supernatant and a protein size standard into the wells of the gel.
g. Set the power supply to a constant 120 V.
h. Run the gel until the migration front reaches roughly the middle of the gel.
i. Stain the gel with Coomassie brilliant blue staining solution.
j. Using a razor blade, cut each lane into three equal slices.
k. Cut each slice into ~1 mm³ cubes to improve reagent penetration.
l. Transfer all cubes from each slice into a separate 2 mL Eppendorf tube.

steps.title: Wash, reduce, alkylate, and digest gel pieces
steps.instruction: Perform sequential washes, reduction, alkylation, digestion, and peptide extraction from the gel cubes, adjusting volumes if needed, and dry the combined peptide extracts.

substeps.instruction: a. Wash gel pieces with 400 µL washing buffer A for 10 min in a thermomixer at 800 g, RT; discard supernatant.
b. Wash with 400 µL washing buffer B for 10 min at 800 g, RT; discard supernatant.
c. Repeat steps a–b four additional times (total of five washes with each buffer).
d. Incubate gel pieces with 200 µL reduction buffer for 20 min at 800 g, RT; discard supernatant.
e. Add 200 µL alkylation buffer, incubate 30 min at 800 g, RT in the dark; discard supernatant.
f. Add 200 µL washing buffer B, incubate 10 min at 800 g, RT; discard supernatant.
g. Add 150 µL digestion buffer (trypsin) to the gel pieces.
h. Incubate 16 h at 37 °C for overnight digestion.
i. Stop digestion by adding 15 µL stop buffer (final 0.1 % formic acid).
j. Transfer the supernatant to a fresh 2 mL Eppendorf tube.
k. Add 150 µL ST buffer C to the gel pieces, incubate 30 min at 800 g, RT.
l. Pool the supernatant from step j with the extract from step k.
m. Dry the pooled peptide solution in a speed‑vac for 2 h at 45 °C.
n. (Caution) If Coomassie dye remains, repeat washing step (b) three additional times.
o. (Caution) Keep gel pieces wet; if they absorb all buffer, add 50 µL extra digestion buffer and adjust stop buffer to maintain 0.1 % formic acid.
p. Pause point: Dried peptides may be stored at –20 °C for up to 1 week.

steps.title: Clean up digested peptides with C18 tip
steps.instruction: Acidify the digest, bind peptides to C18 discs packed in a pipette tip, wash, elute, snap‑freeze, and lyophilize the purified peptides.

substeps.instruction: a. Adjust the pH of the peptide solution to <3 by adding ST buffer A (≈50 µL).
b. Punch out two 16‑gauge Octadecyl (C18) discs with a flat‑tip needle.
c. Insert the two discs into a GPS200 pipette tip using PEEK tubing.
d. Add 20 µL ST buffer A to the tip; centrifuge 1 000 × g for 1 min.
e. Add 20 µL ST buffer C; centrifuge 1 000 × g for 1 min.
f. Add 20 µL ST buffer B; centrifuge 1 000 × g for 1 min.
g. Repeat steps e–f two more times (total three washes with ST buffer B).
h. Load the acidified peptide sample onto the tip.
i. Centrifuge the tip at 1 000 × g for 3 min to bind peptides.
j. Wash bound peptides with 20 µL ST buffer B; centrifuge 1 000 × g for 1 min.
k. Repeat the wash (step j) three times.
l. Elute peptides with 50 µL ST buffer C; collect eluate in a measurement plate.
m. Snap‑freeze the eluate and lyophilize in a speed‑vac.
n. Pause point: Purified peptides can be stored at –80 °C for up to 1 month.

steps.title: Inject peptides into LC‑MS/MS
steps.instruction: Quantify peptide concentration, then inject 0.2–0.5 µg of each sample into the LC‑MS/MS system, using the same amount for all samples.

substeps.instruction: a. Measure peptide amount with Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit.
b. Adjust the injection volume to deliver 0.2–0.5 µg (e.g., 0.1 µg is sufficient for a Q Exactive HF).
c. Load the calculated volume onto the nano‑HPLC coupled to the mass spectrometer.

steps.title: Process raw data with MaxQuant
steps.instruction: Run MaxQuant (v1.6.17.0) on the LC‑MS/MS files using the detailed parameter set provided, keeping all default settings unchanged except those listed.

substeps.instruction: a. Set version to 2.0.1.0, include contaminants, enable PSM/Protein/Site FDR 0.01.
b. Use normalized ratios for occupancy, minimum peptide length 7, minimum scores 0 (unmodified) and 40 (modified), delta score ≥6 for modified peptides.
c. Enable razor and unique peptide counting, label min. ratio count 2, iBAQ disabled.
d. Turn on match‑between‑runs (time window 0.7 min, ion mobility window 0.05), alignment windows 20 min / 1 index.
e. Enable dependent peptide detection, set dependent peptide FDR 0.01.
f. Use fixed modifications: oxidation (M) and protein N‑term acetylation; variable modifications: phosphorylation (STY).
g. Set enzyme to Trypsin/P, specific mode, max missed cleavages 2, multiplicity 2, labeled AAs Lys8 and Arg10.
h. Keep all other MaxQuant parameters at default as listed (e.g., mass ranges, MS/MS tolerances, output tables).
i. Run the analysis on a high‑performance computer (e.g., 72‑core node) to complete processing.

steps.title: Filter MaxQuant output and perform statistical analysis
steps.instruction: Extract required txt files, remove contaminants, select high‑confidence phosphopeptides, normalize, and identify SILAC‑dependent changes using the described criteria.

substeps.instruction: a. Navigate to the combined folder → txt folder; locate proteinGroups.txt, Phospho (STY)Sites.txt, and other relevant files.
b. In proteinGroups.txt and Phospho (STY)Sites.txt, filter out entries marked as contaminants, reverse, or identified only by site.
c. From Phospho (STY)Sites.txt, retain phosphopeptides that have at least two SILAC ratios per sample type and meet: score > 40, localization score > 40, and PEP ≤ 5.
d. Classify retained sites as phosphorylation (positive) or dephosphorylation (negative); discard sites lacking sufficient signal.
e. Compute Z‑scores of LFQ intensity H from proteinGroups.txt to assess protein abundance differences between samples.
f. Discard phosphosites whose abundance changes mirror overall protein abundance changes (same direction).

g. Compare SILAC ratios between MDA‑MB‑231 and NK92‑MI in conjugates; note that NK92‑MI SILAC pairs (only L label) are considered artifacts, while MDA‑MB‑231 H‑label pairs serve as quality control for labeling efficiency.
h. Perform downstream statistical analyses (e.g., t‑tests, volcano plots) as illustrated in Figure 5.

description: Rapid killing of diseased cells, such as cancer cells, by cytotoxic lymphocytes relies on a highly specialized cell-to-cell conjugation termed the immunological synapse. Formation and activity of the immunological synapse involve multiple sequential steps, including but not limited to, recognition of and adhesion to the target cell, integration of signals at the target cell surface driving activation of effector functions, polarization of the lytic machinery toward the target cell and secretion of effector molecules, such as granzyme B and perforin, into the synaptic cleft.1,2,3 Cancer cells have evolved defense responses to evade lymphocyte cytotoxicity, such as rapid polarization of their actin cytoskeleton and vesicles toward the immunological synapse.4,5,6 Characterization of the signaling pathways controlling the key cellular processes at both pre- and post-synaptic sides of the immunological synapse is essential to develop novel strategies aimed at improving cytotoxic lymphocyte immune response. In this protocol we describe the steps for the formation of immunological synapses between natural killer (NK) cells and target cancer cells, the stabilization and isolation of cell-to-cell conjugates, the enrichment and analysis of phospho-peptides by mass spectrometry, and the specific data analysis allowing to unravel phospho-signaling in each cell type. Although the protocol is detailed it is required that the experimenter is familiar with the main techniques used in the protocol, mass spectrometry of peptides, the analysis of proteomics data, and FACS sorting. The protocol can be used with less than 25 μg starting material because of the high efficiency of the preparation and the accuracy of the analysis. Although exemplified for the analysis of the lytic synapse between NK cells and tumor cells, our protocol could, in principle, apply to other types of immunological synapses, such as those involving T cells, dendritic cells, or B cells.1,7,8,9 The main principle
